# Ouro (LoopLM): Scaling Latent Reasoning via Looped Language Models

English · [简体中文](../zh/2510.25741.md) · [Back to the list](../../README.md)

> Pre-train a weight-tied layer stack that repeats 4 times, with a learned exit gate, on 7.7T tokens; the authors report that the 1.4B and 2.6B models match dense models of up to 12B parameters.

**Category**: Depth control · **Status**: draft (numbers not yet re-checked) · **Impact**: cites 269 · HF upvotes 146 · HN points 84

[paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.25741) · [project](https://ouro-llm.github.io) · [weights](https://huggingface.co/ByteDance/Ouro-1.4B)

## Problem

LLMs mostly learn to reason through explicit chain-of-thought added after pre-training. The paper asks whether looping shared layers in latent space, built into pre-training at multi-trillion-token scale, scales better than non-recursive Transformers.

## Method

- Repeat the whole decoder stack (24 layers for 1.4B, 48 for 2.6B) with shared weights; after every step an LM head computes a loss and an exit gate predicts the probability of stopping.
- Stage I minimizes the per-step losses weighted by the gate's exit distribution minus an entropy bonus, which equals a KL term toward a uniform prior over exit steps up to a constant.
- Stage II freezes the LM and trains only the gate to continue while the next step still lowers the loss by more than a threshold; at inference the model exits at the first step whose cumulative exit probability reaches q.
- Pre-train on 7.7T tokens in four stages (8 steps in Stage 1a, then 4; the 2.6B model is upcycled from the 24-layer model), then run reasoning SFT on about 8.3M examples for the Thinking models.

## Loop layout

| Facet | Value |
|---|---|
| Where the loop sits | whole stack |
| Weight sharing | fully tied |
| Passes in training | learned / adaptive |
| Passes at test time | adaptive exit / routing |
| Input injection | none |
| KV cache | per-pass KV |
| Gradient through passes | full BPTT |
| Origin | trained from scratch |
| FFN | dense FFN |
| Attention in the loop | full attention |
| Passes (whole stack (2.6B: 48 layers)) | train 8 in Stage 1a, then 4; test 4 by default; the exit gate can stop earlier |

The whole decoder stack loops: Ouro 1.4B repeats its 24 layers and Ouro 2.6B its 48 layers, which were upcycled from the 24 layers by layer duplication; embedding and LM head sit outside the loop. The embedding enters only before the first step, and each step takes the previous step's output. After every step an LM head and an exit gate read the hidden state. Training always runs T_max steps and weights each step's loss by the learned exit distribution. Each step keeps its own KV cache.

## Other findings

- Training with 8 recurrent steps in Stage 1a led to loss spikes and gradient oscillations, so the authors cut to 4 steps from Stage 1b on. (Section 4.3)
- The trained depth is not always best for the Thinking models. The 1.4B model scores higher at T=5 than at T=4 on OlympiadBench (72.30 vs 71.55) and SuperGPQA (48.73 vs 47.37), and the 2.6B model peaks at T=3 on AIME 2024 (70.33, against 64.70 at T=4). (Tables 12-13)
- Safety on HEx-PHI improves as the number of recurrent steps grows (tested 1-8), including the extrapolated steps 5-8. At 4 steps the harmful rate is 0.009 for Ouro 1.4B Thinking and 0.003 for Ouro 2.6B Thinking (Qwen3-4B-Thinking 0.009). (Section 7.1; Figure 8a)
- On MMLU, the gate with Stage II exit training reaches 66% accuracy at an average of 2.5 exit rounds, against about 64% for the gate from pre-training alone; fixed-depth exit gives 40% at 1 round and 67.35% at 4. (Section 5.4.1; Figure 5)
- Reusing KV caches during prefill costs more than 10 points on GSM8K, so all four steps keep their own KV during prefill. (Section 5.4.2)
- On the synthetic Capo task, looped (4 steps) and non-looped models with the same parameter count both store about 2 bits of knowledge per parameter. (Section 6.1; Figure 6 (left))
- In 20B-token FineWeb-Edu runs at 53M-1.36B, a Standard model with unshared layers and the same executed depth scores higher than LoopLM in every case, and the gap grows with the step count (in Table 18 the 1.3B gap is 0.017 at 2 steps and 0.025 at 4). (Appendix D.1; Table 18)

## Comparison

- **Baseline**: Public dense base models run through the same evaluation pipeline (Gemma3, Llama3.1/3.2, Qwen2.5 and Qwen3, 1B to 12B); the Thinking models are compared with Qwen3 and DeepSeek-Distill-Qwen.
- **Held fixed**: none
- **Differs**: N (unique parameters), D (training tokens)
- **Baseline hyperparameters**: not stated
- **Headline claim**: Ouro 1.4B R4 (7.7T tokens) matches or beats the 4B Qwen3-Base (36T tokens) on BBH (71.02 vs 70.95), GSM8K (78.92 vs 72.86) and MATH500 (82.40 vs 59.60); Ouro 2.6B R4 scores 55.73 on MMLU-Pro, 80.46 on BBH and 90.85 on MATH500, against 53.72, 77.65 and 62.30 for the 8B Qwen3-Base. (Section 5.1; Tables 7-8)

## Caveats

- The headline comparisons (Tables 7-9) are against separately trained public models that differ in parameters and training tokens (2T-36T); no budget is matched, and Ouro runs its stack 4 times per token.
- The models are trained at 4 steps; base benchmark scores are strongest around T=4 and degrade moderately at T=5-8, and the Thinking models degrade at T=6-8 (Tables 10-13).
- By default every step keeps its own KV cache (4× memory at 4 steps); last-step-only reuse was tested for decoding only, because prefill needs all four caches (Section 5.4.2).
- Reasoning results come from an in-house harness with an LLM judge and temperature 1.0, top_p 0.7 for every model (Section 5.2; Table 17).
- Controlled looped-versus-unlooped studies are small; they use synthetic tasks (Capo with 1M-40M GPT-2-style models, Mano, multi-hop QA) and 53M-1.36B models trained on 20B FineWeb-Edu tokens (Section 6; Appendix D).
- The authors did not run exhaustive learning-rate sweeps (Section 4.3), and RLVR with DAPO and GRPO did not improve on the SFT checkpoint (Section 4.5).
